[[File:Jessica-chapman.URSI Group.jpg|thumb|Steinberg (2nd row, 2nd from left) at conference of the [[International Union of Radio Science]], Sydney 1952]]
'''Jean-Louis Steinberg''' (1922–2016) was one of the main pioneers of [[radio astronomy]] in France. In 1953 he was a co-founder of the project to create the [[Nançay Radio Observatory|''Station de Radioastronomie de Nançay'']]<ref name=obit>{{cite web|author=Combes, Michel|author2=Lequeux, James|title=Death of Jean-Louis Steinberg, astronomer at the Paris Observatory|date=5 February 2016|website=l'Observatoire de Paris|url=https://www.observatoiredeparis.psl.eu/IMG/article_PDF/Death-of-Jean-Louis-Steinberg_a3381.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.lemonde.fr/disparitions/article/2016/02/02/jean-louis-steinberg-astronome-de-l-observatoire-de-paris-est-mort-a-93-ans_4857856_3382.html |title=Jean-Louis Steinberg, astronome de l'Observatoire de Paris, est mort à 93 ans |newspaper=Le Monde.fr |date=2 February 2016 }}</ref> (which opened in 1956).

== Biography ==
Jean-Louis Steinberg had a 3 years older brother, a 13 years younger brother, and a sister who died shortly after birth. In [[World War I]], their father was wounded at the [[Battle of Verdun]] and awarded the ''[[Croix de Guerre]]''. Until he was 14 years old, J.-L. Steinberg attended the [[École alsacienne]]. In 1937 he began studying at the [[Lycée Saint-Louis]]. After passing a qualifying examination, he enrolled at [[Sorbonne University]]. There in 1941 he joined the French Communist Party and the Resistance. In 1943 his younger brother was taken in as a lodger by a farming family in Normandy. In 1944 J.-L. Steinberg graduated with a doctorate in engineering from the [[École normale supérieure (Paris)|ENS Paris]] college of Sorbonne University. In June 1944, he, his parents, and his older brother were all rounded up because of their Jewish ethnicity. On July 4th, the family arrived in [[Auschwitz-Birkenau]]. Of the 4 family members, J.-L. Steinberg was the only survivor seven months later. J.-L. Steinberg's younger brother was never deported to a concentration camp and also survived.<ref name=Legacy>{{cite web|title=The Legacy of Jean-Louis Steinberg|author=Couturier, Pierre|date=3 November 2007|url=https://jlsworkshop.sciencesconf.org/data/pages/Discours_PCouturier_EN.pdf}} (14 pages)</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://catalogue.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/cb39298294g |isbn=9782950986634 |title=Des quatre, un seul est rentré : La destruction d'une famille en 1940-1945 |date=2004 |publisher=Association des anciens élèves de l'École alsacienne }}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://collections.ushmm.org/search/catalog/irn507935 |title=Oral history interview with Jean Louis Steinberg - Collections Search - United States Holocaust Memorial Museum }}</ref> J.-L. Steinberg married Madeleine White in 1946. They adopted his younger brother and had a son, Alain, in 1948.<ref name=Legacy/>

At his return in France in 1945, Steinberg, working with [[Jean-François Denisse]] under the influence of [[Yves Rocard]], developed radio astronomy in France. Steinberg and Denisse were the co-founders in 1953 of the [[Paris Observatory]]'s radio astronomy station in Nançay. Steinberg played a major part in the construction of the large decimeter radio telescope,<ref name=IAU>{{cite web|author=Lequeux, James|url=https://www.iau.org/administration/membership/individual/9856/ |title=Obituary. Jean-Louis Steinberg|website=International Astronomical Union (IAU) }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://adsabs.harvard.edu/full/1961AnAp...24...45P|bibcode=1961AnAp...24...45P |title=Réseau à seize antennes fonctionnant sur 9300 MHZ à la Station Radioastronomique de Nançay |last1=Pick |first1=Monique |last2=Steinberg |first2=J. -L. |journal=Annales d'Astrophysique |date=1961 |volume=24 |pages=45–53 }}</ref> which was officially inaugurated in May 1965 by [[Charles de Gaulle]]<ref name=Legacy/> but became fully operational only in 1967.<ref name=IAU/>

In 1963 Steinberg founded in 1963 the Paris Observatory's ''Service d’Astronomie Spatiale'' (service of space astronomy) in Meudon. The service launched, in 1965 and 1967, two French [[Rubis (rocket)|Rubis rocket]]s with low-frequency receivers and with deployment of very long dipole antennas for detection in space of radio waves with frequency less than 3 [[MHz]]. He was the originator of the Stereo-1 experiment on board the Soviet [[Mars 3]] mission launched in 1971. The experiment successfully showed for the first time the directivity of [[Solar radio emission#Solar radio bursts|solar radio burst]]s of Types I and III. A similar experiment for detection at lower frequencies was launched in 1973 on board the Soviet [[Mars 7]] mission.<ref name=IAU/>

From 1962 to 1969, J.-L. Steinberg was the editor-in-chief of the journal ''Annales d’Astrophysique''. His editorial work was assisted by his wife Madeleine, who spoke English and Russian fluently.<ref name=IAU/> In April 1968 astronomers and astrophysicists from several European countries agreed to merge their various astronomical and astrophysical journals into a single European astronomical journal.<ref name=Blaauw>{{cite journal|author=Blaauw, Adriaan|author-link=Adriaan Blaauw|title=Astronomy and Astrophysics: a European Journal, its History and Present Status|journal=Europhysics News|volume=6|issue=12|year=1975|pages=3–5|doi=10.1051/epn/19750612003 |url=https://www.europhysicsnews.org/articles/epn/pdf/1975/12/epn19750612p3.pdf}}</ref> J.-L. Steinberg, Jean-François Denisse, [[Jean-Claude Pecker]], [[Jan Oort]], Anders Reiz, and [[Stuart Pottasch]] played important roles in the founding of the journal.<ref name=Legacy/> The first edition of the resulting journal, ''[[Astronomy & Astrophysics]]'', was published in 1969 with Steinberg and Pottasch as the two co-editors-in-chief. The journal ''Astronomy and Astrophysics'' merged five scientific journals as of January 1969, with a sixth (the Swedish journal ''Arkiv för Astronomi'') merged somewhat later.<ref name=Blaauw/><ref>{{cite journal|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.172.3982.451|doi=10.1126/science.172.3982.451 |title=European Astronomers Decide to Consolidate Their Journals |date=1971 |last1=Steinberg |first1=J. L. |journal=Science |volume=172 |issue=3982 |pages=451–452 |pmid=17758078 |bibcode=1971Sci...172..451S |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Steinberg was a co-editor-in-chief from 1969 to 1973, when he resigned in favor of Jean Heidmann (1923–2000).<ref name=Blaauw/><ref>{{cite journal|title=Jean Heidmann (1923–2000)|author=Shostak, Seth|author-link=Seth Shostak|date=December 2000|journal=Physics Today|volume=53|issue=12|page=85|doi=10.1063/1.1341931 |url=https://pubs.aip.org/physicstoday/article/53/12/85/411073/Jean-Heidmann}}</ref>

Jean-Louis Steinberg wrote a 12-page, English-language autobiography, published in 2001,<ref>{{cite journal|author=Steinberg, Jean-Louis|title=The scientific career of a team leader|journal=Planetary and Space Science|volume=5|issue=49|year=2001|pages=511–522|doi=10.1016/S0032-0633(00)00162-8 |bibcode=2001P&SS...49..511S }}</ref> and coauthored several papers on French radio astronomy published in the ''[[Journal of Astronomical History and Heritage]]'' from 2007 to 2011.<ref name=IAU/>

In 1979 the [[Société Française de Physique]] (SFP) awarded him the [[Prix Félix-Robin]].<ref>{{cite web|language=fr|title=Prix Félix Robin - Société Française de Physique|url=https://sfpnet.fr/prix/prix-felix-robin|website=sfpnet.fr |date=10 April 2025 }}</ref> In November 2017 a workshop was held as a memorial to him, and, on the Paris Observatory's Meudon campus, a building was named after him.<ref>{{cite web|title=International Workshop on Solar, Heliospheric and Magnetospheric Radioastronomy: The legacy of Jean-Louis Steinberg (1922-2016), 6-10 November, Observatorie de Paris, Meudon (France)|url=https://jlsworkshop.sciencesconf.org}}</ref> The asteroid [[13499 Steinberg]] is named in his honour.
